
# Angles, Projections, and Dot Products

## Finding the angle between two vectors

If we think of vectors as arrows with length and direction, it is natural to ask
what that angle between two vectors is.  If that angle is 0, the two fectors point in the 
same direction.  If it is 180 degrees, they point in opposite directions.  If it is
90 degrees, then they are perpendicular.  (In linear algebra, we will use the term
**orthogonal** instead of prependicular.)

But how can we determine the angle between two vectors?

![What is that angle between $\xvec$ and $\yvec$?](images/projection-line-1.pdf){width=40%}

To make life a little easier, let's try to compute $\cos \theta$ instead of $\theta$.
Once we have $\cos \theta$, we can use a computer or calculator to convert this into 
the angle $\theta$ if we like. But often it is sufficient -- sometimes better -- 
to know the cosine of the angle.

:::{.callout-note}
In data science applications, 
the cosine of the angle between two vectors is often called the **cosine similarity**.
It has many applications in machine learning algorithms.
:::

You probably recall that if $\theta$ is an angle in a *right triangle*,
then the cosine of an angle is defined by 

$$
\cos \theta 
= \frac{\mbox{adjacent}}{\mbox{hypotenuse}}
= \frac{\mbox{length of the adjacent side}}{\mbox{length of the hypotenuse}}
$$

So our first step is to get a right triangle involving our angle $\theta$.


{{< pagebreak >}}

## Projections

:::{#def-projection}
The **projection** of a vector $\yvec$ in the direction of a vector $\xvec$, 
which we will denote as $\proj{\yvec}{\xvec}$, 
is the scalar multiple $k \xvec$ of $\xvec$ that makes $\yvec$ and $k\xvec$ 
the hypotenuse and side of a right triangle.
:::


![The projection vector $k\xvec$ forms a right triangle.](images/projection-line-10.pdf){width=20%}

\newcommand{\Num}{\textsf{Num}}

:::{#exr-dot-numerator}
It turns out that our numerator has some nice properties.
Let's temporarily use the notation

$$
\Num(\xvec, \yvec) =  |\yvec| |\xvec| \cos \theta \;.
$$ 

Explain why a--c and e true. (Distributivity is a little trickier. Stay tuned.)

a. **Commutativity**:  $\Num(\xvec, \yvec) = \Num(\yvec, \xvec)$

b. **Scalar multiples**: $k \Num(\xvec, \yvec) = \Num(k \xvec, \yvec) = \Num(\xvec, k \yvec)$

c. **Length**: $\Num(\xvec, \xvec) = \len{\xvec}^2$

d. **Distributivity**: 
$\Num(\xvec, \yvec + \zvec) = \Num(\xvec, \yvec) + \Num(\xvec, \zvec)$
							
e. **Linear Combinations**

    *  $\Num(c_1 \xvec_1 + c_2 \xvec_2, \yvec) = 
    \Num(c_1\xvec_1,\yvec) + 
    \Num(c_2\xvec_2, \yvec)$

    * $\Num(c_1 \xvec_1 + c_2 \xvec_2, d_1\yvec_1 +
				d_2\yvec_2)
				= c_1 d_1 \Num(\xvec_1, \yvec_1) 
				+ c_1 d_2 \Num(\xvec_1, \yvec_2) 
				+ c_2 d_1 \Num(\xvec_2, \yvec_1) 
				+ c_2 d_2 \Num(\xvec_2, \yvec_2)$

:::

## A surprising connection

## Practice

:::{#exr-proj-practice}
For each pair of vectors below, compute $\xvec \cdot \yvec$, $\proj{\xvec}{\yvec}$,
$\proj{\yvec}{\xvec}$, and the cosine of the angle between the two vectors.
For the examples in $\real^2$, illustrate with a figure like the ones above.

a. $\xvec = \twovec 11$, $\yvec = \twovec 10$

b. $\xvec = \twovec 34$, $\yvec = \twovec 11$

c. $\xvec = \fourvec 1111$, $\yvec = \fourvec 1010$

d. $\xvec = \fourvec 1111$, $\yvec = \fourvec 1{-1}1{-1}$

:::

them? What is the dot product of the two vectors?

## More ways to think about the dot product

:::{#exr-dot-as-matrix-product}
a. Show how the dot prduct $\threevec123 \cdot \threevec456$ can be computed
using a matrix product.  What are the matrices?

b. Explain how any dot product $\xvec \cdot \yvec$ can be expressed as a matrix product 
of a  $1 \by n$ matrix with a an $n \by 1$ matrix.  How are the matrices related to
the vectors $\xvec$ and $\yvec$?
:::

:::{#exr-dot-as-linear-trans}
a. Let $T(\xvec) = \xvec \cdot \fourvec1111$. Show that we can think of $T$ as a 
linear transformation. 
What are the domain and codomain of this transformation?

b. Of course, there is nothing special about $\fourvec 1111$.  We can do this with
any vector.

c. There is a nice 
[3Blue1Brown video](https://www.3blue1brown.com/lessons/dot-products) 
about dot prodcuts that
includes illustrations of this connection between the dot prodcut and linear
transformations. I recommend you watch it!
:::
